name: BoofCV
workload: SpeedTestCV example output on one large chessboard JPEG and one binary PNG: BoofCV 0.38-SNAPSHOT under JMH (avgt, 5 iterations, ms/op) against OpenCV Python calls timed by a script (ms per call). Operations: Gaussian blur radius 5, Sobel, local mean threshold radius 5, histogram, Canny edge chains, external contours, Shi-Tomasi corners, polar Hough lines.
claimed_speedup: Mixed result, ratios derived from page data (OpenCV ms divided by BoofCV ms, from the two readme example outputs). BoofCV faster: good features 38.313 ms vs 277.2 ms (7.2x), Hough polar 743.051 ms vs 3086.3 ms (4.2x), histogram 2.268 ms vs 7.0 ms (3.1x), external contour 47.055 ms vs 83.3 ms (1.8x), Sobel 8.010 ms vs 14.0 ms (1.7x). BoofCV slower: Gaussian blur 36.139 ms vs 12.1 ms (OpenCV 3.0x faster), Canny 142.658 ms vs 61.7 ms (OpenCV 2.3x faster), local mean threshold 20.495 ms vs 15.4 ms (OpenCV 1.3x faster). No OpenCV row for SIFT or SURF (SURF not in the pip wheel; SIFT skipped).
compiler_and_flags: BoofCV 0.38-SNAPSHOT (build.gradle), JDK 1.8 and JDK 11 said to give similar output, JMH 1.19; OpenCV side pinned to opencv-python 4.5.1.48 pre-built wheel by opencv/requirements.txt (rule 1 of the benchmark: pre-built binaries only). The OpenCV figures are on https://github.com/lessthanoptimal/SpeedTestCV/blob/master/opencv/readme.md
tradeoffs: Pure Java, runs on the JVM with JIT warm-up. Gaussian blur rounds results (OpenCV truncates with integer division) and RGB-to-gray is a plain average by default (OpenCV uses a weighted average), per the SpeedTestCV readme. Optional OpenCV interop through JavaCV.
caveats: Weak evidence for a catalogue entry in this category: the numbers are 'Example Output' blocks in two sub-readmes of the author's SpeedTestCV repo (no license shown, last commit 2022-07-28), not a published results table; hardware and CPU model are not stated (the BoofCV block says 'On my system'), and the two blocks may come from different runs or machines. BoofCV is timed with JMH (with warm-up), OpenCV with a hand-written Python loop (mean of 10 time.time() trials after gc.collect, one trial for the histogram, no warm-up) in benchmark.py; that loop has cv2.setNumThreads(0) commented out, so OpenCV runs multi-threaded as shipped. The OpenCV Canny row includes a findContours call to produce pixel chains, to match BoofCV's chain output, and the benchmark file itself lists TODOs. BoofCV 0.38-SNAPSHOT and OpenCV 4.5.1 are years old, current BoofCV and OpenCV releases are not retimed. The comparison is not a win overall: OpenCV is 2-3x faster on Gaussian blur and Canny. None of the rows is a colour conversion or resampler, so the assigned category fits only loosely (Gaussian blur and Sobel are the nearest). The author's fuller page, boofcv.org Performance:OpenCV:BoofCV (2012-era, referenced from a BoofCV mailing-list thread seen only as a search result), is blocked in this environment (EGRESS_BLOCKED) and was not read. A 2012 SURF paper by the BoofCV author (title only, not opened; arXiv blocked) reportedly compares SURF runtimes of several implementations; nothing from it is used here. Retier idea for a session with arXiv or boofcv.org access.

name: Canvas-Txt v5
workload: Word-wrap of 600-character lorem-ipsum strings at width 400 px, 16px Arial, 5000 iterations per scenario, node-canvas measureText, three scenarios: same text repeated, 500 strings cycled, never-repeating strings (bench/compare.mjs, calls splitText against canvas-hypertxt split).
claimed_speedup: README table, 600-char strings, µs/op: same text repeated 1.1 (canvas-txt v5) vs 0.9 (canvas-hypertxt, hypertxt faster); 500 strings cycled 5.6 vs 48.3 (about 8.6x, derived from page data); never-repeating strings 51.3 vs 566.2 (about 11.0x, derived from page data). canvas-txt v4: 1,566 / 1,423 / 1,382 µs/op.
compiler_and_flags: Node.js (version not stated; engines >=18), node-canvas ^3.2.3, canvas-hypertxt ^1.0.3 and canvas-txt@4.1.1 per packages/canvas-txt/package.json devDependencies; not a compiled benchmark
tradeoffs: Per-font width cache and bounded memoised layouts (about 500 entries); memoised layouts come back frozen; the cache must be cleared with clearMeasurementCache() after web fonts load. Uses Intl.Segmenter for Unicode-correct breaks (CJK, Thai, emoji). About 4 kB gzipped, zero dependencies.
caveats: Benchmark code is public (packages/canvas-txt/bench/compare.mjs, read in full) but the CPU model, Node version and run-to-run variance are not stated, so tier C rather than A. It times line-wrapping and measurement only (splitText), not drawing, and not node-canvas fillText, so the lead's second baseline is not measured. The README row shows canvas-hypertxt faster on repeated identical text (0.9 vs 1.1 µs/op) and the README admits hypertxt's estimation mode is faster on long never-seen strings. The script clears only canvas-hypertxt's cache between contenders (hyperClearCache), not canvas-txt's own width cache, though each contender gets 100 warm-up iterations. Never-repeating scenario keeps the vocabulary warm. README numbers are for 600 characters; the script also runs 100 and 1000. Lead said issue #13 holds these numbers: it does not, issue #13 is an unrelated request to return the computed text height. The repo's recent commits are co-authored with an AI assistant. Not C++ (TypeScript); baseline is another JavaScript library, so no std comparison applies.

name: vapoursynth-nssfactory (CUDA BM3D)
workload: nss_cuda.BM3D at its default shape (block 8, group 8, sigma 3) on 1080p Gray float clips, default 3 streams, RTX 5080, frames read from VapourSynth's cache; bm3dcuda 'on the same harness'. The repo's docs/api/bm3d.md adds first-party figures for 1080p GRAYS, RTX 5080, one stream, measured 2026-10-06 against bm3dcuda with the same search: about 1.25x spatial with 32 VapourSynth threads, rolling temporal 2.7x at radius 1 and 3.3x at radius 2 with 32 threads (1.4x with one thread), and chroma=1 at YUV444 243, 238 and 229 fps (spatial, radius 1, radius 2) against bm3dcuda chroma=True 200, 94 and 65 fps.
claimed_speedup: PR #23 description: 'bm3dcuda on the same harness: 636 fps; this branch 732 fps at the default 3 streams' (about 1.15x, derived from page data). The same PR reports its own before/after: Gray sigma 3 478 to 710 fps, Gray final 354 to 438 fps, YUV420 344 to 450 fps.
compiler_and_flags: CMake Release, C++20, nvcc from CUDA 12.4 or newer (release packages built with CUDA 12.9); native code for sm_75, sm_86, sm_89 and sm_120 plus compute_75 PTX; flags beyond Release not stated in the PR
hardware: NVIDIA RTX 5080 (1080p); host CPU, driver and VapourSynth version not stated for these runs (the docs name an 'Emerald Rapids core' only for CPU-plugin timings)
tradeoffs: GPL-2.0 (the generated FFTW DCT codelets are GPLv2 or later), work in progress, GPU path needs a CUDA 12.9-capable driver and an NVIDIA GPU; constant Gray/YUV/RGB 32-bit float clips only. CUDA output matches the CPU plugin to 60 dB PSNR or better, not bit-for-bit. Default of 3 streams uses more device and pinned memory than one.
caveats: First-party numbers in a PR body and in docs/api/bm3d.md; the timing harness that produced the 636 fps bm3dcuda figure is not in the repo (tests/cuda_compare.py checks bm3dcuda PSNR, not speed; tools/ holds only a codelet generator), CPU, driver, bm3dcuda build (cuda or rtc variant) and bm3dcuda parameters are not stated, so tier C. The gain over bm3dcuda is modest at the default (1.15x) and the docs say it is bound by frame transfers in the spatial case, where kernels take the same time as bm3dcuda; the larger 2.7x and 3.3x wins are for the rolling temporal mode with 32 threads. The PR also shows the author's own before/after speedups from the same change (1.49x Gray), so the bm3dcuda gap is recent: it was produced by PR #23 merged 2026-10-05. Repository is a few days old in its visible history (first visible commit 2026-10-04) and the README says the project is WIP; numbers may change quickly. Also reports of PSNR improving 73.5 to 138.9 dB on its worst case after the change, so earlier output had larger numeric error.

name: scany (multi-threaded scanner, srwiley)
baseline: srwiley/scanFT ScanFT (Go port of the FreeType/golang freetype CL-AA gray antialiaser, same algorithm as FreeType ftgrays)
workload: Rendering SVG icons through oksvg and rasterx with ScanS (single thread) or ScanT (multi-thread) as the rasterx.Scanner; the repo's Go benchmarks (scant_test.go, scans_test.go) render a set of landscape icons and a gradient-heavy TestShapes6.svg (50 draws per run) at 1x and 5x scale with 1 to 32 threads.
claimed_speedup: No numbers. README: 'ScanS appears to be within 1 or 2 percent as fast as ScanFT'; 'If ScanT is run using a thread count of one it is around 10% slower than ScanFT or ScanS. However, as additional threads are added it will exceed the speed of the single thread implementations'; SVGs with gradients 'particularly benefit from using multiple threads'.
tradeoffs: ScanT starts three kinds of worker thread (cell splitting, cover and area, sweep) and a thread count of N starts N of each, all of which must be shut down with Close(); needs rasterx and oksvg; output via a Collector interface, only an image.RGBA collector is provided. Licensed MIT, while ScanFT is under the FreeType licence because it is a direct port of the C code.
caveats: No measured results anywhere in the repo or README, so the speedup is a prose claim (tier D). The benchmarks in scant_test.go and scans_test.go only vary ScanT's thread count and ScanS; the ScanFT and x/image/vector calls are commented out or absent, so none of the named baselines is timed. The README's own claim for single-threaded ScanS is parity (within 1-2 percent), not a win; only ScanT at several threads is said to be faster, with no hardware, Go version or crossover thread count. The lead's other baselines (golang.org/x/image/vector, scanx, FreeType ftgrays itself) are not compared; ScanFT is the nearest relative of ftgrays. Repository is one star, last commit 2022-01-17, 'go 1.17' module, so it is old and unmaintained. Kept at tier D because the instructions require a record for each listed project.

name: clownresampler
baseline: libsamplerate (nearest incumbent; no baseline is named or timed by the project)
workload: None measured. Single-header C89 audio resampler using integer 16.16 fixed-point positions and a Lanczos-windowed sinc kernel (1024 samples per lobe table), low-level and streaming high-level APIs.
claimed_speedup: None. The README is three sentences (single-file library, C89, 0BSD, windowed-sinc with Lanczos window) and the header comments make no speed claim and name no other library.
tradeoffs: Zero-Clause BSD, single header, no dependencies, written in C89; integer 16.16 fixed-point positions and 17.15 fixed-point normalisation (the repo description says integer-only). In the high-level API the downsampling ratio must not be wider than the one given at init. Only a Lanczos kernel, not the quality ladder of libsamplerate or soxr. The source has a TODO about a remaining per-output-frame division ('divisions are slow').
caveats: No numbers and no comparison against libsamplerate, soxr or speexdsp anywhere: the repo has only functional tests (test-high-level.c and test-low-level.c decode FLAC or MP3 and resample, no timing code), no benchmark directory, and no commit message about speed. Search found no third-party benchmark. Recorded at tier D only because the instructions require one record per listed project; the lead's soxr and speexdsp baselines are untested. Notability is low (37 stars), so this entry is a candidate to drop from a list of faster code unless a measured comparison appears.
